ChuaAugust 4, 2026013 mins Share Post Viber Email While Human Papillomavirus (HPV), a sexually transmitted virus, causes the majority of cervical cancer in women, it is also responsible for various cancers in men. Today, approximately 42 million Americans are infected with HPV, with about 13 million new infections yearly. In the Philippines, about 1.15 to 1.5 million Filipino women carry an active HPV at any given time, and about 38 million to 39.6 million are considered at risk for developing complications. Over the past decades, an estimated “260,000 to 270,000 HPV-associated cancers were diagnosed in women, and 210,000 to 230,000 among men, in the United States over the past decade,” according to the US CDC. These are all preventable with the Gardasil vaccines, when boys and girls are vaccinated before they are sexually active. The rate of throat cancer in the United States has not declined, compared to most head and neck malignancies. I suspect that the statistics could also be true, when extrapolated, for other countries, like the Philippines, since most Filipinos are westernized in their lifestyle, habits, and behaviors, etc. The most logical explanation why cancer of the throat has not diminished has been attributed to the Human Papillomavirus. HPV is popularly known to cause genital and most cancers of the cervix (mouth of the womb). It has only been recently that scientists discovered and identified HPV transmission through oral sex as an etiology of throat cancer. M.D. Anderson Cancer Center in Houston reported that its research team found “the incidence of throat cancer (in the United States) to be stagnant and even rising in some populations, defying a downward trend in other head and neck cancers linked more closely with smoking.” The American Cancer Society reports that the greatest risk factors in head and neck cancers are smoking and drinking alcoholic beverages, 90% of them either smokers or tobacco-chewers and about 80% of them also imbibed a lot of alcohol. The good news is that a trend analysis in head and neck cancers in the United States shows a decline over the past twenty years, trailing a decrease in smoking prevalence, which started in the 1970s, by 10 to 15 years. The bad news is that oropharyngeal cancers (which include the tonsils, base of the tongue and soft palate, and side and back of the throat) have been up in some populations in the United States, and probably among people in other parts of the world who practice oral sex, where HPV takes its toll. HPV could also cause cancer of the vagina, penis, and anus, besides cervical and throat cancers. The sample of the vaccine referred to is Gardasil, which is genetically engineered and which blocks infection caused by two of the more than 100 types of Human Papillomavirus (HPV), strains 16 and 18. These two sexually-transmitted viruses are responsible for about 70% of cervical cancers. HPV, in one form or the other, afflicts more than 20 million Americans. The other strains of the virus cause painful genital warts, and sometimes, cervical cancers too. Let us momentarily discuss cervical cancer, since the HP virus is implicated in its causation in almost three-quarters of this malignancy. How prevalent is cervical cancer? In the Philippines, there are about 5000 new cases of cervical cancer each year. However, more alarming than that is the fact that there are between 10,000 to 25,000 women walking around (not seen by a physician) who have undiagnosed pre-invasive lesions in their cervix. If diagnosed early, these women could be saved. For every four survivors of breast cancer, there are fewer than 3 women who survive cervical cancer, which shows how virulent cervical cancer is. What causes cervical cancer? Human Papillomavirus (HPV, also known as genital herpes virus) accounts for most cervical cancers. At least 50% of sexually active men and women are infected with genital HPV, especially those with multiple partners. Among the million American and Philippine men and women infected with HPV, many linked with abnormal Papare tests, genital warts, and cervical cancer. It is estimated that at least 13 million new cases of cervical cancers are discovered annually. Between half a million and a million Americans have genital warts, transmitted through sexual contact. It takes time for those infected with HPV to develop into cancer, so there are countless infected people out there who would potentially have cancers. The best for children (before turning 10) and adults up to age 45 is to get vaccinated to prevent HPV infection to begin with. Is the cure for cervical cancer? Better than the cure! A vaccine (Gardasil) that prevents cervical cancer, vulvar and vaginal cancer that was approved by the US-FDA in 2006 was found to be “effective 100%, in the short term, at blocking the cancer and lesions likely to turn to cancer” (like the pre-invasive lesions), according to Gardasil manufacturer, Merck. To have 100 percent efficacy is something we see very rarely. The UK’s version of the vaccine is known as Cervarix. How early should the vaccine be given? Students in grammar school, middle school and high school should be vaccinated before they become sexually active, as early as 9 years old for both boys and girls, and adults up to age 45, because once they catch HPV infection, there is no cure; herpes is for life. This was the recommendation of Dr. Gloria Bachmann, director of The Women’s Health Institute at Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in Brunswick, NJ, who said this vaccine is a “phenomenal breakthrough.” Prophylaxis Gardasil vaccination comprehensively eliminates HPV 16 and 18-associated non-invasive and invasive cervical cancer. The vaccine also cuts down infection with HPV 6 and 11, the causes of 90% of genital warts. Gardasil is safe for both boys and girls and adults. How about throat cancers? Of the 45,000 head and neck cancers in the US each year, about 10,000 of them are oropharyngeal cancers, and tongue cancers among young adults have also increased. The evident conclusion is that the cause is the HP virus. “Over the last five years, 35% of the throat cancer patients treated at the M.D. Anderson Cancer Center had no history of smoking, and that close to 90% of patients who had never smoked showed evidence of oral infection with HPV. The researchers felt that “vaccinating only females against HPV could result in a missed opportunity to prevent throat cancers.” It is recommended for both girls and boys to close that gap, preventing boys from spreading the HPV virus. The use of cling plastic wrap used in the kitchen placed over the woman’s groin for oral sex as a shield has been advocated by some to prevent HPV transmission. Mouth, tongue, and other throat cancers could be as grave and deadly as most other forms of cancer. I do not know how to put this more seriously, more effectively, and more delicately, but medically speaking, a moratorium on oral sex might be in order. Realistically, human nature usually prevails. This is a greater argument for childhood vaccination with the life-saving Gardasil. And parents should not deny their sons and daughters this valuable vaccine. * * * The opinions, beliefs and viewpoints expressed by the author do not necessarily reflect the opinions, beliefs and viewpoints of the Asian Journal, its management, editorial board and staff. * * * Philip S. analysis.time: The article was published on 2026-08-04. It discusses HPV-related cancer statistics from the past decade and mentions a trend analysis over the past twenty years.
analysis.location_and_population: The article focuses on the Filipino-American community in the United States, particularly in Arizona, Hawaii, Midwest, Northwest Texas, California, Los Angeles County, San Diego County, and Northern California Nevada Las Vegas. news.content_title: Single dose of HPV vaccine may offer same protection as two doses to prevent cervical cancer: Study
news.content: 3 Min Read A single dose of the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine, which protects against a virus that can cause cervical cancer and several other cancers, may work just as well as the standard two-dose schedule, according to a new study. The study, funded by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and published in the New England Journal of Medicine, was led by Dr Aimee Kreimer of the National Cancer Institute (NCI), part of NIH, and Dr Carolina Porras of the Agencia Costarricense de Investigaciones Biomedicas in Costa Rica. HPV is a common virus that spreads through sexual contact. While most HPV infections go away on their own, some types of the virus can lead to cervical cancer. HPV can also cause cancers of the throat, anus, penis, vagina and vulva, as well as genital warts. For years, doctors have recommended two doses of the HPV vaccine for adolescents. But the new study found that one dose provides the same level of protection. The study involved more than 20,000 girls aged 12 to 16 in Costa Rica, who were enrolled between November 2017 and February 2020. Researchers also surveyed more than 3,000 unvaccinated women and girls to estimate HPV infection levels among those who had not received the vaccine. Participants were randomly divided into groups. They received either one dose of a bivalent HPV vaccine or a nonavalent HPV vaccine. Six months after the first vaccination, half of the participants received a second dose of the same HPV vaccine, while the other half received a vaccine against tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis as a comparison group. The researchers found that one dose of the HPV vaccine protected against persistent cervical HPV infections that was no worse than protection provided by two doses. The study found that all vaccine schedules were at least 97% effective in preventing persistent infections caused by HPV types 16 and 18. "The findings suggest that a single dose of either HPV vaccine will provide adequate protection against HPV infection and subsequent cervical cancers as effectively as two doses," said Kreimer. The findings could make it easier for millions of girls worldwide to get vaccinated, especially in countries where access to vaccines remains limited. HPV is a common virus that spreads through sexual contact. While most HPV infections go away on their own, some types of the virus can lead to cervical cancer. While many HPV infections clear on their own, certain cancer-causing types of the virus can lead to cervical cancer, which kills around 2.5 lakh women worldwide every year. analysis.brief_en: A large NIH-funded study published in the New England Journal of Medicine suggests that a single dose of HPV vaccine may provide the same protection against persistent cervical HPV infections as the standard two-dose regimen. The randomized trial, conducted in Costa Rica with more than 20,000 girls aged 12–16, found at least 97% effectiveness against HPV types 16 and 18 across all dosing schedules. HPV causes cervical cancer and other malignancies, yet global vaccination coverage among adolescent girls remains below 30%. If confirmed, the findings could simplify delivery and expand access, particularly in low-resource settings where two-dose completion is challenging.

news.title_zh: 单剂 HPV 疫苗 可能提供与两剂相同的保护以预防 宫颈癌:研究
news.source_body_en: A large NIH-funded study published in the New England Journal of Medicine suggests that a single dose of HPV vaccine may provide the same protection against persistent cervical HPV infections as the standard two-dose regimen. The randomized trial, conducted in Costa Rica with more than 20,000 girls aged 12–16, found at least 97% effectiveness against HPV types 16 and 18 across all dosing schedules. HPV causes cervical cancer and other malignancies, yet global vaccination coverage among adolescent girls remains below 30%. If confirmed, the findings could simplify delivery and expand access, particularly in low-resource settings where two-dose completion is challenging.
news.content_zh: 发表在《新英格兰医学杂志》上的一项由 NIH 资助的大型研究表明,单剂 HPV 疫苗 可以提供与标准两剂方案相同的针对持续性宫颈 HPV 感染的保护作用。这项在哥斯达黎加对 20,000 多名 12-16 岁女孩进行的随机试验发现,在所有给药方案中,针对 HPV 16 和 18 型的有效性至少为 97%。HPV 会导致 宫颈癌 和其他恶性肿瘤,但全球青少年女孩中 疫苗接种 的覆盖率仍低于 30%。如果得到证实,这些发现可以简化给药并扩大可及性,特别是在资源匮乏的环境中,完成两剂疫苗具有挑战性。

news.content: Skip to main content Your source for the latest research news Follow: Facebook X/Twitter Subscribe: RSS Feeds Newsletter New! Sign up for our free email newsletter. Science News from research organizations Cancer-fighting chewing gum cuts HPV levels by up to 93% Bioengineered chewing gum may offer a surprisingly powerful new way to fight microbes linked to head and neck cancer. Date: August 4, 2026 Source: University of Pennsylvania Summary: A specially engineered chewing gum reduced HPV by up to 93% and nearly eliminated two bacteria linked to head and neck cancer. The treatment preserved beneficial mouth bacteria, raising hopes for a safer and more affordable therapy. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY Researchers developed a bioengineered chewing gum that sharply reduced three microbes linked to head and neck cancers. Credit: Shutterstock Researchers have developed a bioengineered chewing gum that may offer a new way to target microbes associated with head and neck cancer. In tests involving oral samples from patients, extracts from the gum sharply reduced one virus and two types of bacteria linked to the disease. The research team was led by Henry Daniell of the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The findings were published in Scientific Reports and could support the development of more accessible and affordable treatments. A Need for Better Head and Neck Cancer Therapies Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that begins in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. The disease can be particularly aggressive, and outcomes are often poor when it is discovered at a later stage. Daniell says that many recently approved cancer medications have not produced major improvements in patients' quality of life or five-year survival. That limited progress highlights the need for new approaches that can work alongside existing treatments. Targeting HPV and Harmful Oral Bacteria The new study builds on earlier research involving chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). The gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring antiviral protein. Daniell and his colleagues used oral samples from patients with HNSCC to study three microbes associated with cancer. These included human papillomavirus, or HPV, along with two bacterial species, Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn). "The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies." Gum Extracts Sharply Reduce Microbe Levels Tests showed that extracts from the bean gum lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples. HPV levels also fell by 80% in oral rinse samples. The researchers then engineered the bean gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide capable of killing harmful bacteria. A single dose brought levels of Pg and Fn down to almost zero. Importantly, the treatment did not appear to harm the beneficial bacteria that normally live in the mouth. Radiation therapy can have a different effect, reducing helpful bacteria while encouraging the growth of disease-causing yeast (Candida albicans). A Potential Addition to Cancer Treatment The ability to target dangerous microbes while preserving the healthy oral microbiome could make the gum useful in several ways. Researchers believe it may eventually serve as an additional therapy alongside current cancer treatments or as a preventive measure against infection and transmission. "Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission." Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. Other authors include Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System. The research received support from NIH (grant 5-R01-HL 107904-13 awarded to Henry Daniell), the Academic Senate Grant of the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA (the Surgical Education Research program), and the National Cancer Institute Cancer Center (Support Grant P30 CA168524). The treatment preserved beneficial mouth bacteria, raising hopes for a safer and more affordable therapy. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY Researchers developed a bioengineered chewing gum that sharply reduced three microbes linked to head and neck cancers. Credit: Shutterstock Researchers have developed a bioengineered chewing gum that may offer a new way to target microbes associated with head and neck cancer. In tests involving oral samples from patients, extracts from the gum sharply reduced one virus and two types of bacteria linked to the disease. The research team was led by Henry Daniell of the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. The findings were published in Scientific Reports and could support the development of more accessible and affordable treatments. A Need for Better Head and Neck Cancer Therapies Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a common form of cancer that begins in the tissues lining the mouth and throat. The disease can be particularly aggressive, and outcomes are often poor when it is discovered at a later stage. Daniell says that many recently approved cancer medications have not produced major improvements in patients' quality of life or five-year survival. That limited progress highlights the need for new approaches that can work alongside existing treatments. Targeting HPV and Harmful Oral Bacteria The new study builds on earlier research involving chewing gum made from lablab beans (bean gum). The gum contains FRIL, a naturally occurring antiviral protein. Daniell and his colleagues used oral samples from patients with HNSCC to study three microbes associated with cancer. These included human papillomavirus, or HPV, along with two bacterial species, Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg) and Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn). "The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection," says Daniell. "And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant, or supplemental, therapies." Gum Extracts Sharply Reduce Microbe Levels Tests showed that extracts from the bean gum lowered HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples. HPV levels also fell by 80% in oral rinse samples. The researchers then engineered the bean gum to contain protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide capable of killing harmful bacteria. A single dose brought levels of Pg and Fn down to almost zero. Importantly, the treatment did not appear to harm the beneficial bacteria that normally live in the mouth. Radiation therapy can have a different effect, reducing helpful bacteria while encouraging the growth of disease-causing yeast (Candida albicans). A Potential Addition to Cancer Treatment The ability to target dangerous microbes while preserving the healthy oral microbiome could make the gum useful in several ways. Researchers believe it may eventually serve as an additional therapy alongside current cancer treatments or as a preventive measure against infection and transmission. "Lip and oral cavity cancer was the seventh leading cancer type in cancer incidence and mortality rate worldwide in adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults in 2022," says Daniell. "Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission." Henry Daniell is the W.D. Miller Professor in the Department of Basic & Translational Sciences at the School of Dental Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania. Other authors include Geetanjali Wakade, Rahul Singh, and Smruti Nair of Penn Dental Medicine; Andrés M. Bur and Sufi M. Thomas of the University of Kansas Medical Center; Eri S. Srivatsan and Marilene B. Wang of the University of California at Los Angeles; and Saroj K. Basak of the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System. The research received support from NIH (grant 5-R01-HL 107904-13 awarded to Henry Daniell), the Academic Senate Grant of the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA (the Surgical Education Research program), and the National Cancer Institute Cancer Center (Support Grant P30 CA168524). analysis.time: Event date: Not reported in the supplied evidence. Publication date: 4 August 2026 (N4).
analysis.location_and_population: University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine, United States (N9, N30).
analysis.event: A bioengineered chewing gum engineered to contain antiviral and antibacterial agents was reported to reduce human papillomavirus (HPV) levels in oral samples from patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), alongside reductions in two bacteria linked to HNSCC (Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum). The findings were published in Scientific Reports and presented as a potential adjunct therapy or preventive measure (N16, N18, N20-N23, N26, N27, N40, N41).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: HPV levels reduced by 93% in saliva samples and 80% in oral rinse samples; Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum levels reduced to nearly zero after a single dose. The treatment preserved beneficial oral bacteria. No explicit risk level was stated in the evidence (N20-N24).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study used ex vivo clinical samples from HNSCC patients. The gum was engineered with FRIL (antiviral protein) and protegrin (antimicrobial peptide). Authors propose advancing to clinical trials as an adjuvant therapy or prophylaxis. Funding sources include NIH, UCLA Academic Senate, and NCI Cancer Center Support Grant. No human trials, regulatory approvals, or clinical implementation details were reported (N17, N22, N26, N27, N29, N36, N41).

Findings published in Scientific Reports follow ex vivo testing on patient samples and highlight the need for new approaches to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, where outcomes remain poor at later stages. The team calls for advancing the therapy to clinical trials.

news.content_title: CDA Consult calls for greater focus on cervical cancer prevention, urges support for free HPV vaccination
news.content: Home Radio TV Videos Movies Advertise Ghana Contact Login NEWS SPORTS BUSINESS POLITICS OPINIONS HEALTH AFRICA WORLD ENTERTAINMENT LIFESTYLE SCIENCE TECHNOLOGY NOLLYWOOD MEDIA MEMBERS Archive Health News Family/Parenting Home/Food Health/Fitness Spirituality OnAIR Search CDA Consult calls for greater focus on cervical cancer prevention, urges support for free HPV vaccination By Kristodia Otibu Asiedu II Contributor Health MON, 03 AUG 2026 Executive Director of CDA Consult, Mr. Francis Ameyibor The Communication for Development and Advocacy Consult (CDA Consult) has called for intensified national efforts to combat cervical cancer, urging stakeholders to give the disease the same level of attention and public advocacy as breast cancer. The organisation stressed that tackling women's cancers requires a comprehensive approach that combines sustained breast cancer awareness with stronger education on cervical cancer prevention. Speaking during a media engagement in Koforidua in the Eastern Region over the weekend, the Executive Director of CDA Consult, Mr. Francis Ameyibor, said promoting awareness of both diseases would strengthen prevention efforts and create “a shield for generations,” by equipping women and girls with the knowledge needed to safeguard their long-term health. He noted that although breast cancer receives significant public attention during annual awareness campaigns, cervical cancer—despite being largely preventable through regular screening and Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination—continues to receive limited public education. According to him, the lack of awareness, stigma associated with gynaecological examinations and limited access to routine screening in some communities have contributed to late diagnosis and avoidable deaths among women. Mr. Ameyibor urged the media to play a leading role in promoting cervical cancer awareness, noting that many women delay seeking medical attention until the disease has reached an advanced stage. “Many women only seek medical attention when symptoms have advanced, reducing the chances of successful treatment,” he said. He called on media organisations, civil society groups, faith-based organisations and community health stakeholders to join a coordinated advocacy campaign promoting regular medical check-ups, early screening and HPV vaccination. Mr. Ameyibor reaffirmed CDA Consult's commitment to mobilising health professionals, traditional and religious leaders, government institutions and civil society organisations to intensify efforts aimed at eliminating cervical cancer in Ghana. He said integrating cervical cancer education into mainstream public health campaigns would provide women with accurate information and encourage early detection and treatment. The Executive Director also appealed to parents and guardians to ensure that eligible girls receive the HPV vaccine, describing it as one of the most effective interventions for preventing cervical cancer later in life. He said CDA Consult would continue to promote cervical cancer awareness through community outreach programmes, media partnerships, workplace education and digital advocacy campaigns. Mr. Ameyibor welcomed the government's decision to introduce the HPV vaccine into Ghana's routine immunisation programme for girls aged nine years and acknowledged the support of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, UNICEF, the World Health Organization (WHO) and other development partners. He noted that the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign, scheduled to begin in September, targets girls between the ages of nine and 14 and represents a major milestone in Ghana's efforts to eliminate cervical cancer by 2030. According to him, CDA Consult has since 2023 been implementing a nationwide Change Paradigm Advocacy Campaign for Free HPV Vaccination to promote prevention, early detection and treatment of cervical cancer. He explained that the organisation regularly brings together health professionals, human rights advocates, gender activists, religious leaders and communication practitioners to educate the public on cervical cancer prevention and broader health issues. The advocacy campaign, he said, combines calls for free HPV vaccination with sustained public education on screening, diagnosis and treatment. Mr. Ameyibor noted that the campaign is being carried out under the national theme, "Ghana Must Rise Against Cervical Cancer," with regional-specific slogans and advocacy strategies designed to strengthen public education across the country. “Our team will work with regional health professionals to embark on vigorous education across the districts to ensure that the message to combat cervical cancer through vaccination, screening, diagnosis and treatment is spread across,” he said. He described the inclusion of the HPV vaccine in Ghana's national immunisation schedule as a major breakthrough in the country's fight against cervical cancer. “As holistic health advocates, CDA Consult is pleased for the nationwide initiative and more delighted for the government has adopted the HPV vaccination into the national routine immunization schedules for girls; this is a major breakthrough,” Mr. Ameyibor noted. news.content_original: Home Radio TV Videos Movies Advertise Ghana Contact Login NEWS SPORTS BUSINESS POLITICS OPINIONS HEALTH AFRICA WORLD ENTERTAINMENT LIFESTYLE SCIENCE TECHNOLOGY NOLLYWOOD MEDIA MEMBERS Archive Health News Family/Parenting Home/Food Health/Fitness Spirituality OnAIR Search CDA Consult calls for greater focus on cervical cancer prevention, urges support for free HPV vaccination By Kristodia Otibu Asiedu II Contributor Health MON, 03 AUG 2026 Executive Director of CDA Consult, Mr. Francis Ameyibor The Communication for Development and Advocacy Consult (CDA Consult) has called for intensified national efforts to combat cervical cancer, urging stakeholders to give the disease the same level of attention and public advocacy as breast cancer. The organisation stressed that tackling women's cancers requires a comprehensive approach that combines sustained breast cancer awareness with stronger education on cervical cancer prevention. Speaking during a media engagement in Koforidua in the Eastern Region over the weekend, the Executive Director of CDA Consult, Mr. Francis Ameyibor, said promoting awareness of both diseases would strengthen prevention efforts and create “a shield for generations,” by equipping women and girls with the knowledge needed to safeguard their long-term health. He noted that although breast cancer receives significant public attention during annual awareness campaigns, cervical cancer—despite being largely preventable through regular screening and Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination—continues to receive limited public education. According to him, the lack of awareness, stigma associated with gynaecological examinations and limited access to routine screening in some communities have contributed to late diagnosis and avoidable deaths among women. Mr. Ameyibor urged the media to play a leading role in promoting cervical cancer awareness, noting that many women delay seeking medical attention until the disease has reached an advanced stage. “Many women only seek medical attention when symptoms have advanced, reducing the chances of successful treatment,” he said. He called on media organisations, civil society groups, faith-based organisations and community health stakeholders to join a coordinated advocacy campaign promoting regular medical check-ups, early screening and HPV vaccination. Mr. Ameyibor reaffirmed CDA Consult's commitment to mobilising health professionals, traditional and religious leaders, government institutions and civil society organisations to intensify efforts aimed at eliminating cervical cancer in Ghana. He said integrating cervical cancer education into mainstream public health campaigns would provide women with accurate information and encourage early detection and treatment. The Executive Director also appealed to parents and guardians to ensure that eligible girls receive the HPV vaccine, describing it as one of the most effective interventions for preventing cervical cancer later in life. He said CDA Consult would continue to promote cervical cancer awareness through community outreach programmes, media partnerships, workplace education and digital advocacy campaigns. Mr. Ameyibor welcomed the government's decision to introduce the HPV vaccine into Ghana's routine immunisation programme for girls aged nine years and acknowledged the support of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, UNICEF, the World Health Organization (WHO) and other development partners. He noted that the nationwide HPV vaccination campaign, scheduled to begin in September, targets girls between the ages of nine and 14 and represents a major milestone in Ghana's efforts to eliminate cervical cancer by 2030. According to him, CDA Consult has since 2023 been implementing a nationwide Change Paradigm Advocacy Campaign for Free HPV Vaccination to promote prevention, early detection and treatment of cervical cancer. He explained that the organisation regularly brings together health professionals, human rights advocates, gender activists, religious leaders and communication practitioners to educate the public on cervical cancer prevention and broader health issues. The advocacy campaign, he said, combines calls for free HPV vaccination with sustained public education on screening, diagnosis and treatment. Mr. Ameyibor noted that the campaign is being carried out under the national theme, "Ghana Must Rise Against Cervical Cancer," with regional-specific slogans and advocacy strategies designed to strengthen public education across the country. “Our team will work with regional health professionals to embark on vigorous education across the districts to ensure that the message to combat cervical cancer through vaccination, screening, diagnosis and treatment is spread across,” he said. He described the inclusion of the HPV vaccine in Ghana's national immunisation schedule as a major breakthrough in the country's fight against cervical cancer. “As holistic health advocates, CDA Consult is pleased for the nationwide initiative and more delighted for the government has adopted the HPV vaccination into the national routine immunization schedules for girls; this is a major breakthrough,” Mr. Ameyibor noted.
